turns.doctor_question: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I'm here because... I just can't stop focusing on this rough, sunken-looking patch on my face. 

Whenever I look in the mirror, or, you know, see a picture of myself, it's all I can see. It just makes one side of me look real old and... beat-up. The thing is, people keep telling me they barely notice anything at all, but I see it, and it's just really getting to me.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes an intense preoccupation with a perceived rough, sunken patch on their face that others say they barely notice, which is the hallmark of preoccupation with appearance.

turns.doctor_question: When other people tell you they don't really notice anything, do you ever feel they might be right, or are you completely convinced that it is as severe and noticeable as you see it?
turns.patient_response:
I don't really know. Sometimes I try to tell myself that maybe they're right, you know? Like, maybe I'm making too big a deal out of it. But... then I look in the bathroom mirror and it's just right there. It's so obvious to me. 

So I guess most of the time, I'm pretty convinced it really is that bad. I usually just figure people are trying to be polite, or maybe they just aren't looking at me that close.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes being convinced of a physical flaw that is obvious to them in the mirror, despite others saying they don't notice it, indicating a preoccupation with a perceived defect.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself spending a lot of time doing things like repeatedly checking the mirror, trying to cover it up, or comparing your face to other people?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, I do. Especially before I head out to the job site, or if I'm supposed to go to my sister's place for game night. I'll just stand there in the bathroom, checking the mirror over and over. I turn my head this way and that, trying to see it under different lights, you know? 

Sometimes I catch myself just rubbing at the spot, like maybe I can smooth it out or something. If it's looking real bad to me, I'll pull my work hat down low to try and cast a shadow over it. And... well, sometimes if I think it's just too obvious, I'll just make up an excuse and not go out at all.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms engaging in repetitive behaviors such as checking the mirror over and over, rubbing the perceived flaw, and using a hat to camouflage it.
